GENERAL DEMAND LETTER (INFORMAL)
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Inc.

PURPOSE, SENDER, AND RECIPIENT
This is a demand letter from Jordan Alex Lee to Acme Inc. A demand letter is a written communication commonly used to state a request to another person or business, in writing, before pursuing other options. This letter sets out Jordan Alex Lee's own account of the relevant facts and Jordan Alex Lee's own request. It is not a pleading filed with any court, not a determination by any court or government agency, and it does not by itself commence a lawsuit or any other legal proceeding.

CALIFORNIA'S DEBT-COLLECTION STATUTE AND WHETHER IT REACHES A PERSON COLLECTING THEIR OWN DEBT
California's principal debt-collection statute, the Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (Civil Code § 1788 et seq.), imposes significant restrictions on a "debt collector." The Act's own definition of that term is "any person who, in the ordinary course of business, regularly, on behalf of himself or herself or others, engages in debt collection" — wording that, unlike the federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, does not exclude a person collecting a debt owed to that person. California courts have held that the Rosenthal Act's definition of "debt collector" is, for that reason, far broader than the federal Act's, which specifically excludes a person collecting a debt that person originated. Whether sending a letter like this one about a debt makes the sender a "debt collector" subject to the Rosenthal Act's restrictions therefore does not turn only on whether the sender is the original creditor rather than a third-party collector; it turns instead on whether the sender's debt-collection activity is conducted "in the ordinary course of business" and "regularly" — a question about the sender's own pattern of activity that this document does not resolve. Separately, the Act's substantive protections apply only to a "consumer debt" — money due from a natural person because of a consumer credit transaction — so a debt that does not fit that description is outside the Act's definition regardless of who is collecting it.

  "The terms “consumer debt” and “consumer credit” mean money, property or their equivalent, due or owing or alleged to be due or owing from a natural person by reason of a consumer credit transaction."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1788.2(f) (law.onecle.com mirror of California Civil Code text), California Civil Code, the Act's substantive protections are limited to "consumer debt" (https://law.onecle.com/california/civil/1788.2.html)

The Rosenthal Act does not mirror the FDCPA, and clearly does not do so with respect to the definition of “debt collector.”"
  — Davidson v. Seterus, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist., Div. 1, Mar. 13, 2018, No. D071502) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Court of Appeal, holding the Rosenthal Act's "debt collector" definition is far broader than the FDCPA's, which excludes a person collecting a debt that person originated (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4476953/davidson-v-seterus-inc/)

THE LINE BETWEEN A LAWFUL DEMAND AND CRIMINAL EXTORTION
California's extortion statute identifies specific kinds of threats that can constitute extortion, including a threat to accuse the person threatened of a crime, or to expose or impute to that person a deformity, disgrace, or crime. A separate statute makes it a crime to send a letter expressing or implying such a threat with intent to extort property or other consideration. The California Supreme Court has explained that a demand letter asserting a legal claim, and stating an intention to pursue a lawsuit if the claim is not resolved, is not by itself extortion: "rude, aggressive, or even belligerent prelitigation negotiations, whether verbal or written, that may include threats to file a lawsuit, report criminal behavior to authorities or publicize allegations of wrongdoing" do not "necessarily constitute extortion." What the court held did cross that line, on the facts before it, was a demand for payment conditioned on withholding an accusation of a crime or on not exposing a disgrace — using the threat of exposure or accusation itself, rather than the underlying legal claim, as the leverage for payment.

  — Cal. Penal Code § 519 (law.onecle.com mirror of California Penal Code text), California Penal Code, kinds of threats that can constitute extortion (https://law.onecle.com/california/penal/519.html)
  "Every person who, with intent to extort property or other consideration from another, sends or delivers to any person any letter or other writing, whether subscribed or not, expressing or implying, or adapted to imply, any threat such as is specified in Section 519 is punishable in the same manner as if such property or other consideration were actually obtained by means of such threat."

  "We emphasize that our conclusion that Mauro’s communications constituted criminal extortion as a matter of law are based on the specific and extreme circumstances of this case. Extortion is the threat to accuse the victim of a crime or “expose, or impute to him . . . any deformity, disgrace or crime” (Pen. Code, § 519) accompanied by a demand for payment to prevent the accusation, exposure, or imputation from being made. Thus, our opinion should not be read to imply that rude, aggressive, or even belligerent prelitigation negotiations, whether verbal or written, that may include threats to file a lawsuit, report criminal behavior to authorities or publicize allegations of wrongdoing, necessarily constitute extortion."
  — Flatley v. Mauro, 39 Cal.4th 299, 332, fn. 16 (2006) (opinion text via CourtListener), California Supreme Court, distinguishing ordinary prelitigation demand letters from criminal extortion (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2600567/flatley-v-mauro/)

Flatley's own footnote 16 — the source of the "rude, aggressive, or even belligerent" quotation above — expressly states that its holding that the communications at issue were extortion "as a matter of law" rests on "the specific and extreme circumstances of this case," so California law has not reduced this boundary to a bright-line test that resolves every case; the court's own list of what does not necessarily cross the line is illustrative, not exhaustive, and the reverse — what reliably does cross it, short of Flatley's own facts — is even less settled. STATEMENT OF FACTS
Jordan Alex Lee describes the relevant facts, in Jordan Alex Lee's own words, as follows:

On September 3, 2026, I paid a $500 deposit for event-planning services. The event was cancelled by the business on September 10, 2026, and no refund has been issued since.

The description above reflects Jordan Alex Lee's own understanding and account of events. It is not a finding or determination by any court, agency, or other decision-maker, and nothing in this letter states that Acme Inc. has any particular legal obligation to Jordan Alex Lee.

REQUESTED ACTION, AMOUNT, AND DEADLINE
Based on the facts described above, Jordan Alex Lee requests that Acme Inc. take the following action by December 15, 2026: Refund the $500 deposit in full.

If this request includes a specific dollar amount, that amount is: $500.00.

This section states Jordan Alex Lee's own request. It is not an invoice, bill, or order issued by any court, and December 15, 2026 is a date chosen by Jordan Alex Lee, not a deadline set by statute or by any court, except to the extent some other deadline independently applies to the underlying facts described above.

IF THE DEADLINE PASSES
If Acme Inc. does not respond to, or comply with, this request by December 15, 2026, next steps Jordan Alex Lee may consider include, without limitation, renewing or revising this request, pursuing informal resolution, filing an action in small claims court or another court of appropriate jurisdiction, or any other lawful remedy available under California law. Nothing in this letter states that any particular option will be pursued, or that pursuing any option would result in a particular outcome. This letter does not waive any right or remedy Jordan Alex Lee may have, all of which are expressly reserved, whether or not specifically described in this letter.

SIGNATURE
Jordan Alex Lee
By: _______________________
Date: _______________

Sent to:
Acme Inc.
